questions.q: A shop's expected number of orders is 1.1 per day. What does that mean?
options: Most days the shop gets exactly 1.1 orders
1.1 is the most likely number of orders
Averaged over many days, orders come to about 1.1 per day, even though no single day can have 1.1 orders
The shop never gets more than 1.1 orders
questions.why: The mean is a probability-weighted average, not a promised or most likely value; here it is not even a possible value. Treating the mean as the most likely outcome is a common misreading.

questions.q: X takes the value 0 with probability 0.5, 2 with probability 0.3 and 4 with probability 0.2. What is the mean of X?
questions.why: Mean = 0 × 0.5 + 2 × 0.3 + 4 × 0.2 = 0 + 0.6 + 0.8 = **1.4**. 2 is the simple average of the three values, which ignores that 0 is far more likely than 4.

questions.q: For the same X (0 with probability 0.5, 2 with 0.3, 4 with 0.2; mean 1.4), what is the standard deviation?
questions.why: Variance = (0 − 1.4)² × 0.5 + (2 − 1.4)² × 0.3 + (4 − 1.4)² × 0.2 = 0.98 + 0.108 + 1.352 = 2.44, so SD = √2.44 ≈ **1.56**. 2.44 is the variance, in squared units; 4.4 is the average of X² before subtracting the squared mean.

questions.q: Orders per day have mean 1.1 and SD 0.7. Each order earns ₹250 and the day has a fixed cost of ₹150, so profit = 250X − 150. What are the mean and SD of daily profit?
questions.why: Mean: 250 × 1.1 − 150 = **₹125**. SD: only the scaling matters, 250 × 0.7 = **₹175**. Subtracting the fixed cost from the SD (giving ₹25) is the trap: a fixed amount shifts the mean but adds no uncertainty.

questions.q: Delivery times are roughly normal with mean 45 minutes and SD 10 minutes. If you promise delivery within 65 minutes, about what share of deliveries will break the promise?
questions.why: 65 minutes is two SDs above the mean. About 95% fall within ±2 SD, leaving 5% split between the two tails, so roughly **2.3%** are later than 65 minutes. 5% counts both tails, but early deliveries do not break the promise; 16% would be the share beyond one SD (55 minutes).

questions.q: A salesperson makes 5 calls a day; each converts independently with probability 0.3. What is the probability of at least one sale in a day?
questions.why: This is binomial. P(no sale) = 0.7⁵ ≈ 0.168, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.168 ≈ **0.832**. 1.5 is the mean (5 × 0.3), not a probability; 0.002 is 0.3⁵, the chance that all five calls convert.

questions.q: Delivery time is a continuous random variable. What is the probability that a delivery takes exactly 30.000… minutes?
options: The height of the density curve at 30
0; for continuous variables you ask about ranges, such as between 29 and 31 minutes
1 divided by the number of possible times
It equals the probability of 30 orders in the discrete case
questions.why: Individual exact values of a continuous variable have zero probability; probabilities are areas under the density curve over a range. Reading the curve's height as a probability is the common mistake: a density can even exceed 1.

questions.q: Interview: "Two suppliers both average 5 days to deliver. Why might you still prefer one?" Which answer is best?
options: You would not; equal means make them equivalent
Their spread can differ: a supplier delivering in 4 or 6 days (SD 1) needs less safety stock than one delivering in 2 or 8 days (SD 3), so variance has a rupee cost
Prefer the one with the higher variance, because it is sometimes faster
Only the median matters for supply planning
questions.why: Planning has to cover the bad days, so stock is set by the spread as well as the average: 6 days of cover for the reliable supplier, 8 for the erratic one. Judging on the mean alone hides that risk; occasional fast deliveries do not offset the slow ones you must stock for.
